The Sole Commendation He Needs to Prove God's Sanction of His Ministry He Has in His Corinthian Converts: His Ministry Excels the Mosaic, as the Gospel of Life and Liberty Excels the Law of Condemnation.<div eID="gen34157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17209"/>1. Are we beginning again to recommend ourselves (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.12">2Co 5:12</reference>) (as some of them might say he had done in his first Epistle; or, a reproof to "some" who had begun doing so)!<div eID="gen34158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commendation--</hi>recommendation. (Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.18">2Co 10:18</reference>). The "some" refers to particular persons of the "many" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>) teachers who opposed him, and who came to Corinth with letters of recommendation from other churches; and when leaving that city obtained similar letters from the Corinthians to other churches. The thirteenth canon of the Council of Chalcedon (A.D. 451) ordained that "clergymen coming to a city where they were unknown, should not be allowed to officiate without letters commendatory from their own bishop." The history (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.27">Ac 18:27</reference>) confirms the existence of the custom here alluded to in the Epistle: "When Apollos was disposed to pass into Achaia [Corinth], the brethren [of Ephesus] wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him." This was about two years before the Epistle, and is probably one of the instances to which Paul refers, as many at Corinth boasted of their being followers of Apollos (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>). <div eID="gen34159" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17210"/><div sID="gen34160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17210"/><hi type="bold">2. our epistle--</hi>of recommendation.<div eID="gen34160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in our hearts--</hi>not letters borne merely in the hands. Your conversion through my instrumentality, and your faith which is "known of all men" by widespread report (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4-1Cor.1.7">1Co 1:4-7</reference>), and which is written by memory and affection on my inmost heart and is borne about wherever I go, is my letter of recommendation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.2">1Co 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen34161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known and read--</hi>words akin in root, sound, and sense (so <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.13">2Co 1:13</reference>). "Ye are known to be my converts by general knowledge: then ye are known more particularly by your reflecting my doctrine in your Christian life." The handwriting is first "known," then the Epistle is "read" [Grotius] (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Co 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.25">1Co 14:25</reference>). There is not so powerful a sermon in the world, as a consistent Christian life. The eye of the world takes in more than the ear. Christians' lives are the only religious books the world reads. Ignatius [Epistle to the Ephesians, 10] writes, "Give unbelievers the chance of believing through you. Consider yourselves employed by God; your lives the form of language in which He addresses them. Be mild when they are angry, humble when they are haughty; to their blasphemy oppose prayer without ceasing; to their inconsistency, a steadfast adherence to your faith." <div eID="gen34162" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17211"/><div sID="gen34163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17211"/><hi type="bold">3. declared--</hi>The letter is written so legibly that it can be "read by all men" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2Co 3:2</reference>). Translate, "Being manifestly shown to be an Epistle of Christ"; a letter coming manifestly from Christ, and "ministered by us," that is, carried about and presented by us as its (ministering) bearers to those (the world) for whom it is intended: Christ is the Writer and the Recommender, ye are the letter recommending us.<div eID="gen34163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God--</hi>Paul was the ministering pen or other instrument of writing, as well as the ministering bearer and presenter of the letter. "Not with ink" stands in contrast to the letters of commendation which "some" at Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>) used. "Ink" is also used here to include all outward materials for writing, such as the Sinaitic tables of stone were. These, however, were not written with ink, but "graven" by "the finger of God" (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.18">Ex 31:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.16">32:16</reference>). Christ's Epistle (His believing members converted by Paul) is better still: it is written not merely with the finger, but with the "Spirit of the living God"; it is not the "ministration of death" as the law, but of the "living Spirit" that "giveth life" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6-2Cor.3.8">2Co 3:6-8</reference>).<div eID="gen34164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not in--</hi>not on tables (tablets) of stone, as the ten commandments were written (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">2Co 3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen34165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in fleshy tables of the heart--</hi>ALL the best manuscripts read, "On [your] hearts [which are] tables of flesh." Once your hearts were spiritually what the tables of the law were physically, tables of stone, but God has "taken away the stony heart out of your flesh, given you a heart of flesh" (fleshy, not fleshly, that is, carnal; hence it is written, "out of your flesh" that is, your carnal nature), <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.19">Eze 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.26">36:26</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2Co 3:2</reference>, "As ye are our Epistle written in our hearts," so Christ has in the first instance made you "His Epistle written with the Spirit in (on) your hearts." I bear on my heart, as a testimony to all men, that which Christ has by His Spirit written in your heart [Alford]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pr 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.3">7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34">Jr 31:31-34</reference>). This passage is quoted by Paley [Horæ Paulinæ] as illustrating one peculiarity of Paul's style, namely, his going off at a word into a parenthetic reflection: here it is on the word "Epistle." So "savor," <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14-2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:14-17</reference>. <div eID="gen34166" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17212"/><div sID="gen34167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17212"/><hi type="bold">4. And--</hi>Greek, "But." "Such confidence, however (namely, of our 'sufficiency,' <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2Co 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">2Co 2:16</reference>--to which he reverts after the parenthesis--as ministers of the New Testament, 'not hinting,' <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">2Co 4:1</reference>), we have through Christ (not through ourselves, compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>) toward God" (that is, in our relation to God and His work, the ministry committed by Him to us, for which we must render an account to Him). Confidence toward God is solid and real, as looking to Him for the strength needed now, and also for the reward of grace to be given hereafter. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.24.15">Ac 24:15</reference>, "hope toward God." Human confidence is unreal in that it looks to man for its help and its reward. <div eID="gen34167" type="x-p"/>

"From" more definitely refers to the source out of which a thing comes; "of" is more general.<div eID="gen34168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to think--</hi>Greek, to "reason out" or "devise"; to attain to sound preaching by our reasonings [Theodoret]. We cannot expect too little from man, or too much from God. <div eID="gen34170" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17214"/><div sID="gen34171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17214"/><hi type="bold">6. able--</hi>rather, as the Greek is the same, corresponding to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2Co 3:5</reference>, translate, "sufficient as ministers" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.7">Ep 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col 1:23</reference>).<div eID="gen34171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the new testament--</hi>"the new covenant" as contrasted with the Old Testament or covenant (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">1Co 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.24">Ga 4:24</reference>). He reverts here again to the contrast between the law on "tables of stone," and that "written by the Spirit on fleshly tables of the heart" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">2Co 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen34172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not of the letter--</hi>joined with "ministers"; ministers not of the mere literal precept, in which the old law, as then understood, consisted; "but of the Spirit," that is, the spiritual holiness which lay under the old law, and which the new covenant brings to light (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.17-Matt.5.48">Mt 5:17-48</reference>) with new motives added, and a new power of obedience imparted, namely, the Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">Ro 7:6</reference>). Even in writing the letter of the New Testament, Paul and the other sacred writers were ministers not of the letter, but of the spirit. No piety of spirit could exempt a man from the yoke of the letter of each legal ordinance under the Old Testament; for God had appointed this as the way in which He chose a devout Jew to express his state of mind towards God. Christianity, on the other hand, makes the spirit of our outward observances everything, and the letter a secondary consideration (<reference osisRef="John.4.24">Joh 4:24</reference>). Still the moral law of the ten commandments, being written by the finger of God, is as obligatory now as ever; but put more on the Gospel spirit of "love," than on the letter of a servile obedience, and in a deeper and fuller spirituality (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.17-Matt.5.48">Mt 5:17-48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.9">Ro 13:9</reference>). No literal precepts could fully comprehend the wide range of holiness which LOVE, the work of the Holy Spirit, under the Gospel, suggests to the believer's heart instinctively from the word understood in its deep spirituality.<div eID="gen34173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">letter killeth--</hi>by bringing home the knowledge of guilt and its punishment, death; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">2Co 3:7</reference>, "ministration of death" (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">Ro 7:9</reference>).<div eID="gen34174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit giveth life--</hi>The spirit of the Gospel when brought home to the heart by the Holy Spirit, gives new spiritual life to a man (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">Ro 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.11">11</reference>). This "spirit of life" is for us in Christ Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.10">10</reference>), who dwells in the believer as a "quickening" or "life-giving Spirit" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">1Co 15:45</reference>). Note, the spiritualism of rationalists is very different. It would admit no "stereotyped revelation," except so much as man's own inner instrument of revelation, the conscience and reason, can approve of: thus making the conscience judge of the written word, whereas the apostles make the written word the judge of the conscience (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1">1Pe 4:1</reference>). True spirituality rests on the whole written word, applied to the soul by the Holy Spirit as the only infallible interpreter of its far-reaching spirituality. The letter is nothing without the spirit, in a subject essentially spiritual. The spirit is nothing without the letter, in a record substantially historical. <div eID="gen34175" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. able-- rather, as the Greek is the same, corresponding to 2Co 3:5 , translate, "sufficient as ministers" ( Ep 3:7 ; Col 1:23 ). the new testament-- "the new covenant" as contrasted with the Old Testament or covenant ( 1Co 11:25 ; Ga 4:24 ). He reverts here again to the contrast between the law on "tables of stone," and that "written by the Spirit on fleshly tables of the heart" ( 2Co 3:3 ). not of the letter-- joined with "ministers"; ministers not of the mere literal precept, in which the old law, as then understood, consisted; "but of the Spirit," that is, the spiritual holiness which lay under the old law, and which the new covenant brings to light ( Mt 5:17-48 ) with new motives added, and a new power of obedience imparted, namely, the Holy Spirit ( Ro 7:6 ). Even in writing the letter of the New Testament, Paul and the other sacred writers were ministers not of the letter, but of the spirit. No piety of spirit could exempt a man from the yoke of the letter of each legal ordinance under the Old Testament; for God had appointed this as the way in which He chose a devout Jew to express his state of mind towards God. Christianity, on the other hand, makes the spirit of our outward observances everything, and the letter a secondary consideration ( Joh 4:24 ). Still the moral law of the ten commandments, being written by the finger of God, is as obligatory now as ever; but put more on the Gospel spirit of "love," than on the letter of a servile obedience, and in a deeper and fuller spirituality ( Mt 5:17-48 ; Ro 13:9 ). No literal precepts could fully comprehend the wide range of holiness which LOVE, the work of the Holy Spirit, under the Gospel, suggests to the believer's heart instinctively from the word understood in its deep spirituality. letter killeth-- by bringing home the knowledge of guilt and its punishment, death; 2Co 3:7 , "ministration of death" ( Ro 7:9 ). spirit giveth life-- The spirit of the Gospel when brought home to the heart by the Holy Spirit, gives new spiritual life to a man ( Ro 6:4 , 11 ). This "spirit of life" is for us in Christ Jesus ( Ro 8:2 , 10 ), who dwells in the believer as a "quickening" or "life-giving Spirit" ( 1Co 15:45 ). Note, the spiritualism of rationalists is very different. It would admit no "stereotyped revelation," except so much as man's own inner instrument of revelation, the conscience and reason, can approve of: thus making the conscience judge of the written word, whereas the apostles make the written word the judge of the conscience ( Ac 17:11 ; 1Pe 4:1 ). True spirituality rests on the whole written word, applied to the soul by the Holy Spirit as the only infallible interpreter of its far-reaching spirituality. The letter is nothing without the spirit, in a subject essentially spiritual. The spirit is nothing without the letter, in a record substantially historical.
entries.reader_content_plain: 6. able-- rather, as the Greek is the same, corresponding to 2Co 3:5 , translate, "sufficient as ministers" ( Ep 3:7 ; Col 1:23 ). the new testament-- "the new covenant" as contrasted with the Old Testament or covenant ( 1Co 11:25 ; Ga 4:24 ). He reverts here again to the contrast between the law on "tables of stone," and that "written by the Spirit on fleshly tables of the heart" ( 2Co 3:3 ). not of the letter-- joined with "ministers"; ministers not of the mere literal precept, in which the old law, as then understood, consisted; "but of the Spirit," that is, the spiritual holiness which lay under the old law, and which the new covenant brings to light ( Mt 5:17-48 ) with new motives added, and a new power of obedience imparted, namely, the Holy Spirit ( Ro 7:6 ). Even in writing the letter of the New Testament, Paul and the other sacred writers were ministers not of the letter, but of the spirit. No piety of spirit could exempt a man from the yoke of the letter of each legal ordinance under the Old Testament; for God had appointed this as the way in which He chose a devout Jew to express his state of mind towards God. Christianity, on the other hand, makes the spirit of our outward observances everything, and the letter a secondary consideration ( Joh 4:24 ). Still the moral law of the ten commandments, being written by the finger of God, is as obligatory now as ever; but put more on the Gospel spirit of "love," than on the letter of a servile obedience, and in a deeper and fuller spirituality ( Mt 5:17-48 ; Ro 13:9 ). No literal precepts could fully comprehend the wide range of holiness which LOVE, the work of the Holy Spirit, under the Gospel, suggests to the believer's heart instinctively from the word understood in its deep spirituality. letter killeth-- by bringing home the knowledge of guilt and its punishment, death; 2Co 3:7 , "ministration of death" ( Ro 7:9 ). spirit giveth life-- The spirit of the Gospel when brought home to the heart by the Holy Spirit, gives new spiritual life to a man ( Ro 6:4 , 11 ). This "spirit of life" is for us in Christ Jesus ( Ro 8:2 , 10 ), who dwells in the believer as a "quickening" or "life-giving Spirit" ( 1Co 15:45 ). Note, the spiritualism of rationalists is very different. It would admit no "stereotyped revelation," except so much as man's own inner instrument of revelation, the conscience and reason, can approve of: thus making the conscience judge of the written word, whereas the apostles make the written word the judge of the conscience ( Ac 17:11 ; 1Pe 4:1 ). True spirituality rests on the whole written word, applied to the soul by the Holy Spirit as the only infallible interpreter of its far-reaching spirituality. The letter is nothing without the spirit, in a subject essentially spiritual. The spirit is nothing without the letter, in a record substantially historical.

The literal translation is, "The ministration of death in letters," of which "engraven on stones" is an explanation. The preponderance of oldest manuscripts is for the English Version reading. But one (perhaps the oldest existing manuscript) has "in the letter," which refers to the preceding words (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>), "the letter killeth," and this seems the probable reading. Even if we read as English Version, "The ministration of death (written) in letters," alludes to the literal precepts of the law as only bringing us the knowledge of sin and "death," in contrast to "the Spirit" in the Gospel bringing us "life" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>). The opposition between "the letters" and "the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8">2Co 3:8</reference>) confirms this. This explains why the phrase in Greek should be "in letters," instead of the ordinary one which English Version has substituted, "written and."<div eID="gen34177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was glorious--</hi>literally, "was made (invested) in glory," glory was the atmosphere with which it was encompassed.<div eID="gen34178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">could not steadfastly behold--</hi>literally, "fix their eyes on." <reference osisRef="Exod.34.30">Ex 34:30</reference>, "The skin of his face shone; and they were AFRAID to come nigh him." "Could not," therefore means here, "for FEAR." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17221"/><div sID="gen34190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17221"/>13. We use no disguise, "as Moses put a veil over his face, that the children of Israel might not look steadfastly upon the end of that which was to be done away" [Ellicott and others]. The view of <reference osisRef="Exod.34.30-Exod.34.35">Ex 34:30-35</reference>, according to the Septuagint is adopted by Paul, that Moses in going in to speak to God removed the veil till he came out and had spoken to the people; and then when he had done speaking, he put on the veil that they might not look on the end, or the fading, of that transitory glory. The veil was the symbol of concealment, put on directly after Moses' speaking; so that God's revelations by him were interrupted by intervals of concealment [ALFORD]. But Alford's view does not accord with <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">2Co 3:7</reference>; the Israelites "could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance." Plainly Moses' veil was put on because of their not having been able to "look steadfastly at him." Paul here (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2Co 3:13</reference>) passes from the literal fact to the truth symbolized by it, the blindness of Jews and Judaizers to the ultimate end of the law: stating that Moses put on the veil that they might not look steadfastly at (Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">Ro 10:4</reference>) the end of that (law) which (like Moses' glory) is done away. Not that Moses had this purpose; but often God attributes to His prophets the purpose which He has Himself. Because the Jews would not see, God judicially gave them up so as not to see. The glory of Moses' face is antitypically Christ s glory shining behind the veil of legal ordinances. The veil which has been taken off to the believer is left on to the unbelieving Jew, so that he should not see (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Is 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.26">Ac 28:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.27">27</reference>). He stops short at the letter of the law, not seeing the end of it. The evangelical glory of the law, like the shining of Moses' face, cannot be borne by a carnal people, and therefore remains veiled to them until the Spirit comes to take away the veil (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14-2Cor.3.17">2Co 3:14-17</reference>) [Cameron]. <div eID="gen34190" type="x-p"/>
